related_questions.question: What is the #1 cause of bankruptcies?

text_blocks.snippet: The #1 cause of bankruptcies in the United States is medical expenses, specifically those stemming from illness or injury, even for individuals with health insurance. These costs can include treatment, medications, and lost income due to time away from work.

While other factors like job loss, overspending, and divorce can also contribute to bankruptcy, medical expenses are consistently cited as the primary driver. A significant number of people file for bankruptcy due to medical debt, even if they have insurance coverage. Studies show that medical issues, both the cost of care and the inability to work due to illness, are major contributors to bankruptcy filings.
Here's a breakdown of why medical expenses are so impactful:

list.title: Unexpected Costs:
list.snippet: Medical emergencies and unexpected illnesses can lead to sudden and substantial bills, even with insurance.

list.title: Insurance Limitations:
list.snippet: Even with insurance, co-pays, deductibles, and uncovered treatments can create significant debt.

list.title: Job Loss and Medical Issues:
list.snippet: A serious illness or injury can lead to job loss, resulting in the loss of income and health insurance, further exacerbating the financial burden.

list.title: Vicious Cycle:
list.snippet: The inability to work due to illness can lead to mounting medical debt, which can then make it harder to recover and return to work.

related_questions.question: What disqualifies you from filing bankruptcies?

text_blocks.snippet: Several factors can disqualify someone from filing for bankruptcy. These include recent bankruptcy discharges, failing the means test, fraudulent activity, failing to complete required credit counseling or debtor education courses, and not paying filing fees. Additionally, certain debts like student loans, child support, and alimony are generally not dischargeable in bankruptcy.
snippet_highlighted_words: recent bankruptcy discharges, failing the means test, fraudulent activity, failing to complete required credit counseling or debtor education courses, and not paying filing fees

list.snippet: There are time limits between bankruptcy filings. For Chapter 7, you must wait eight years from a previous Chapter 7 discharge or six years from a Chapter 13 discharge.
For Chapter 13, the waiting period is two years after a previous Chapter 13 discharge or four years after a Chapter 7 discharge.
The means test determines if your income is low enough to qualify for Chapter 7 bankruptcy. If your income is too high, you may be required to file for Chapter 13 instead.

The test compares your income to the median income for your state and household size. If your income exceeds the median, the court will assess whether you have enough disposable income to repay debts.
Hiding assets, lying on bankruptcy forms, or making fraudulent transfers within a year of filing can disqualify your case.
This includes undervaluing assets, concealing property, or taking out excessive luxury debt shortly before filing.
You must complete a credit counseling course from an approved provider before filing and a debtor education course after filing.
Failure to complete these courses will prevent your case from proceeding.
Certain debts, like student loans (with some exceptions), child support, alimony, and some tax debts, are generally not dischargeable in bankruptcy.
Additionally, debts incurred due to drunk driving or criminal restitution orders are typically not dischargeable.
Bankruptcy filings have associated fees, and failure to pay these fees can result in dismissal of your case.

text_blocks.snippet: 7. Failure to Cooperate with the Bankruptcy Court:

list.snippet: Cooperation with the bankruptcy trustee, including providing accurate financial information and attending hearings, is crucial. Non-cooperation can lead to disqualification, according to Richard West Law Office.

related_questions.question: What will I lose if I file bankruptcy?

text_blocks.snippet: Filing for bankruptcy can lead to the loss of certain assets, especially in Chapter 7 bankruptcy, which involves liquidating assets to repay creditors. However, many people who file for bankruptcy keep most, if not all, of their belongings due to exemptions. These exemptions protect certain types of property, like essential household items, work tools, and in many cases, a primary vehicle and a portion of your home equity.

list.title: Valuable non-exempt assets:
list.snippet: If you own valuable items not covered by exemptions, like a second home, expensive jewelry, or luxury items, you might have to sell them to pay creditors.

list.title: Assets securing debt:
list.snippet: If you have secured debts (like a mortgage or car loan) and are behind on payments, you might lose the property if you can't reaffirm the debt or make arrangements to keep it current.

list.title: Assets not protected by exemptions:
list.snippet: If you have more equity in your home than allowed by your state's homestead exemption, or if you have valuable items not covered by other exemptions, you could lose them.

list.title: Non-dischargeable debts:
list.snippet: Certain debts like student loans, recent taxes, and child support are generally not dischargeable in bankruptcy and will remain your responsibility.
Household goods and personal belongings: Most bankruptcy filers keep their clothing, furniture, appliances, and personal possessions.
Essential tools of the trade: Tools and equipment needed for your job are usually protected.
Retirement accounts: Retirement accounts are often protected by exemptions.
Social Security and other government benefits: These benefits are generally protected.
In many cases, your home and car: Federal and state exemptions allow you to protect some equity in your home and vehicle.

list.title: Chapter 7 vs. Chapter 13:
list.snippet: Chapter 7 bankruptcy is a liquidation process, while Chapter 13 is a reorganization where you make a repayment plan.

list.title: Exemptions vary by state:
list.snippet: Each state has its own set of bankruptcy exemptions, so it's crucial to understand what's protected in your specific state.

list.title: Consult with a bankruptcy attorney:
list.snippet: It's highly recommended to consult with a qualified attorney to assess your specific situation and determine the best course of action. They can help you understand which assets are at risk and how to protect them.
